out.rationale: Christiano et al. state their experiments use a hand-coded decomposer on algorithmic tasks and shed no light on whether humans can decompose real-world tasks. Reppert et al. report human developers iteratively decomposing real science Q&A tasks, raising held-out accuracy (placebo description 25% to 65%, adherence 53% to 70%, Qasper 38% to 69%); the decompositions are hand-designed LM programs, not trained by amplification and distillation.

out.other_title: Is learned task decomposition feasible for hard real-world tasks, and where does it fail?
out.rationale: Wu et al. ask whether decomposition beyond a fixed algorithmic tree is feasible for hard real-world tasks. Reppert et al. report a human-in-the-loop workflow that iteratively refines decompositions of science Q&A tasks, raising held-out accuracy (e.g. Qasper 38% to 69%); the decompositions are designed by developers, not learned by a model, so the 'learned' part of Wu et al.'s question stays open.
out.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether task decompositions for hard real-world tasks can be found and improved, for science Q&A pipelines refined by human developers

text: The authors describe iterated decomposition, a human-in-the-loop workflow for developing compositional LM programs by zooming in on failing components and refining them via decomposition, added context or chain of thought, supported by ICE, an open-source trace visualiser. Applied to three real-world tasks, they report held-out accuracy gains over less compositional baselines: placebo description 25% to 65%, participant adherence 53% to 70%, and Qasper NLP questions 38% to 69%.
title: Iterated decomposition: human-in-the-loop workflow for refining compositional LM programs
